title: two Eids, not one
hook: new clothes, an envelope from an uncle, and the second Eid people forget
tomorrow: the greeting that is a wish

segments.voice: Yesterday: one day of Ramadan, dark to dark. Six words so far: bismillah, al-Fatiha, wudu, inshallah, iman, Ramadan. Today, the seventh.

The morning after Ramadan ends, kids are up early in new clothes. An uncle hands out envelopes of money. The family heads to a prayer held in the morning, and then it's visits, sweets, and Eid Mubarak said so many times it blurs. And yet plenty of people, Muslims included, half forget there's a second Eid a couple of months later, or what makes it different. Today, both.
screen: `NEW CLOTHES. AN ENVELOPE.` → `EID MUBARAK.` → `AND A SECOND EID.`

segments.voice: Eid is tied to a root meaning to return: a day that comes back around, every year. When the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ arrived in Medina, a saying reports, people there had two old days of games and celebration. God has given you two better ones, he told them: the day of breaking the fast, and the day of sacrifice. The first is Eid al-Fitr. Fitr means breaking the fast. It closes Ramadan, and before the Eid prayer, each household gives a small gift of food, zakat al-fitr, so people in need can celebrate too. The second is Eid al-Adha, the feast of sacrifice. It falls during the hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, and it remembers Ibrahim, Abraham, and the ram given in place of his son. Families who are able offer an animal, and share the meat with relatives, neighbors and people in need. So one Eid closes a month of fasting, and the other comes with the pilgrimage. Both begin with a prayer, and both are built so nobody is left out of the feast. And Eid Mubarak? A blessed Eid.
screen: `EID — A DAY THAT COMES BACK AROUND.` · `EID AL-FITR — BREAKING THE FAST.` · `EID AL-ADHA — THE FEAST OF SACRIFICE.` · `NOBODY LEFT OUT OF THE FEAST.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, picture a table set for a feast. On the second, picture who's around it: your people. On the third, add one more chair, for someone who might not have a table of their own today.
Eid. A feast that comes back around: al-Fitr after the fast, al-Adha with the pilgrimage. Seventh word: a week's worth.
Your line: joy that comes back around. That's week one: seven words, and what's inside each. Tomorrow, the greeting that is a wish.

howItsDone: On both Eids Muslims gather in the morning for the Eid prayer, dress in their best, visit family, share food and greet each other with Eid Mubarak; children often get gifts of money. Before Eid al-Fitr each household gives zakat al-fitr, and at Eid al-Adha those able offer an animal and share the meat.

trapdoor: what you thought: one big holiday at the end of Ramadan.
what it means: two Eids — al-Fitr closes Ramadan; al-Adha comes with the pilgrimage and remembers Ibrahim.
what a scholar hears: 'id, from the sense of return; a hadith in Abu Dawud and an-Nasa'i names the two days; zakat al-fitr is due before the Eid prayer; al-Adha recalls 37:102–107.

story.title: the dream and the ram
story.text: An old man tells his young son something terrible: I've seen in a dream that I must sacrifice you. What do you think? The son doesn't run. Father, he says, do what you've been told; God willing, you'll find me patient. As the father lays him down, a voice calls out: you've already fulfilled the vision. A great sacrifice is given in the boy's place.

wrong.myth: Eid is one holiday, at the end of Ramadan.
wrong.truth: there are two: Eid al-Fitr closes Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha comes at the time of the pilgrimage.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 1134; Sunan an-Nasa'i 1556 (two better days: al-Adha and al-Fitr)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1503 (zakat al-fitr, given before people go out to the prayer)
Qur'an 22:36 (eat of them and feed the needy)

notes: NEW lesson (2026-10-06), from the audience research's #7 moment and proposed day 7 ('the two Eids, and what's different'). Ends week one on a celebration. Later lessons go deeper (zakat al-fitr day 126, Eid al-Fitr day 127, Eid al-Adha day 129).
'Eid is tied to a root meaning to return' ('id from 'a-w-d, 'that which returns', Lane): a standard lexical note, stated as 'tied to'. Confirm.

The Medina hadith (Anas: 'Allah has given you something better than them: the day of al-Adha and the day of al-Fitr'): Abu Dawud 1134, an-Nasa'i 1556, cited from memory; graded sahih by many. Confirm.
Zakat al-fitr before the Eid prayer: Bukhari 1503 (Ibn Umar); amounts and forms (food or money) differ between schools and the script gives none. Confirm.

Eid al-Adha: 'remembers Ibrahim and the ram given in place of his son'. The Qur'an doesn't name the son (most Muslims say Isma'il); the script says 'his son'. 'A ram' follows the common understanding of 'a tremendous victim' (37:107). Sharing the meat with relatives, neighbors and the needy follows 22:28 and 22:36; the custom of thirds is common but not universal, so the script doesn't give it. Confirm.
'A couple of months later': Eid al-Adha (10 Dhu al-Hijja) falls about seventy days after Eid al-Fitr (1 Shawwal). Kept vague under the claims rule.

Sensitive: the story card retells Ibrahim's dream (37:102–107) gently and ends at the ransom; a Keeper should confirm it suits day 7, since it is the story every Muslim child knows but is intense for a newcomer. 'God willing' in the son's reply (37:102) links back to day 4.
Moon-sighting debates and the Sunni/Shia Eid prayer details are left out of week one.
Week one rebuilt 2026-10-06 from the audience research; confirm with the Keeper.
